title: Police Powers, FIR and Your Rights
summary: What to do if the police stop, search, question, or arrest you. And how an FIR is different from a complaint.
sectionRefs: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997)

body.text: It is scary when the police stop you or arrest you. If you know a few clear rules, you can stay calm and protect yourself. These rules come from the Constitution and the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS). The BNSS replaced the old CrPC.
🚔 If the police stop you or ask you questions

items: Stay calm and polite. Do not argue and do not run.
You can ask the officer for their name and their police station.
You do not have to answer questions that could be used against you (incriminate you).
During a vehicle check, you must show your licence and documents.
A search usually needs a warrant (a written court order) or a clear legal reason. There are some exceptions, like when you agree, during a lawful arrest, or under a specific law.
If the police search your home, ask for the legal reason. Also ask for independent witnesses to be present.
A woman can be searched only by a woman officer, and with respect.
The police cannot hold you forever. If you are held, ask on what legal basis. Remember the 24-hour rule below.

body.text: 📝 FIR and a police complaint - what is the difference

items: An FIR (First Information Report) is the first formal record of a cognisable offence (a serious crime the police must act on). It is registered at the police station.
For a non-cognisable offence (a less serious crime), you can make a complaint. You can also file it before a Magistrate.
You have the right to a free copy of the FIR.
If the police refuse to register your FIR, you can go to the Superintendent of Police. You can also file a complaint before the Magistrate under the BNSS, or use your state police online portal.
You have the right to know why you are being arrested (Article 22(1)).
You have the right to tell a family member or a friend.
You must be brought before a magistrate within 24 hours (Article 22(2)).
You have the right to a lawyer of your choice. If you cannot afford one, you have the right to free legal aid.
No one can force you to confess. A statement given under threat is not valid (Article 20(3)).

body.text: Normally, a woman cannot be arrested after sunset and before sunrise. There are rare exceptions, with a magistrate's permission and a woman officer present.
You have the right to a medical examination. You also have the right to have your arrest written in a memo signed by a witness.
For a bailable offence, you have the right to be released on bail. The police should tell you this.

items: From 1 July 2024, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC).
Sections 35 to 38 of the BNSS deal with arrest, and with your right to meet an advocate during interrogation (questioning).

body.text: ⏳ Grounds of arrest and the 24-hour rule

items: The grounds of arrest (the reason for the arrest) must be given to you (Constitution Article 22(1); BNSS section 47).
You must be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours of arrest. The journey time is not counted (Article 22(2); BNSS section 58).

body.text: ⚖️ Your right to a lawyer and free legal aid

items: You may consult a lawyer of your choice.
Free legal aid is available. You can call the NALSA helpline 15100, or approach the District Legal Services Authority (DLSA).
A serious offence can be reported at ANY police station. This is called a Zero FIR (BNSS section 173(1) proviso).
The police station then sends it to the station that should handle it.
For a bailable offence, bail is a right.
For a non-bailable offence, the court decides.
Article 20(1): you cannot be punished for an act that was not an offence when you did it.
Article 20(2): you cannot be punished twice for the same offence.
Article 20(3): you cannot be forced to be a witness against yourself.
D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) laid down rules the police must follow.
The police must keep an arrest memo (a written note of the arrest) signed by a witness.
They must inform a family member.
They must arrange a medical examination.
A woman cannot normally be arrested after sunset and before sunrise.
Exception: only with a magistrate's permission and in the presence of a woman officer (BNSS section 43(5)).

body.text: 📝 A free copy of the FIR, and what to do if the police refuse

items: You are entitled to a free copy of the FIR.
If the police refuse to register it, you can go to the Superintendent of Police or the Magistrate.

practicalSteps: Note the time, the place, and the officers' names or badge numbers.
Tell one person you trust where you are and who took you.
Ask for the reason for the arrest, and for a copy of the FIR, in writing.
Do not sign any blank paper or any paper you have not read.
Ask for a lawyer, or call the NALSA helpline 15100 for free legal aid.
exceptions: Preventive detention laws allow the police to hold a person without a normal charge. But there are safeguards and regular reviews.
For some serious offences, an arrest can be made without a warrant. But the 24-hour rule still applies.

faqs.q: Can the police search my phone or home without a warrant?
faqs.a: A search usually needs a warrant or a clear legal reason. There are exceptions, like when you agree, during a lawful arrest, or under a specific law. Ask for the legal reason.

faqs.q: What if the police refuse to register my FIR?
faqs.a: Send your complaint to the Superintendent of Police. Or file a complaint before the Magistrate under the BNSS. Or use your state police online complaint portal. Keep a copy of everything you send.

sources.label: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 - India Code

misconceptions.myth: The police can keep me as long as they want before a court hearing.
misconceptions.fact: No. Under Article 22(2), you must be brought before a magistrate within 24 hours of your arrest.
